message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel, data‑intensive tasks – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each highly optimized for complex control flow, low latency, and large caches. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores, optimized for throughput, with many threads running simultaneously. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set (CISC) with sophisticated branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution, and large cache hierarchies. | Simpler instruction set (often SIMD) that can execute the same operation on many data elements at once. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, high bandwidth memory access, low latency. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on massive memory bandwidth and shared memory pools. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Sequential tasks, branching logic, I/O, operating system services. | Parallelizable tasks like matrix multiplication, image processing, neural network inference/training. |
| **Performance Metrics** | Clock speed (GHz), instructions per cycle (IPC), single‑thread performance. | FLOPS (floating‑point operations per second), memory bandwidth, throughput. |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Optimized for low power per core, but overall power consumption rises quickly with more cores. | Very efficient for throughput‑heavy workloads; can deliver more FLOPS per watt for suitable tasks. |

In short, CPUs excel at handling diverse, sequential tasks with low latency, while GPUs shine when you need to perform the same operation on many data points in parallel, delivering high throughput for specific workloads.
